chief_complaint: pearly white facial nodule with telangiectasias
hpi_details: A 20-year-old female presents with a pearly white facial nodule with telangiectasias, similar to several other small lesions she has had removed from her face and trunk since her early teens. She reports a family history of early-onset skin cancers.
ideas: She thinks the bump is another one of the benign cysts or family skin growths that her relatives frequently get.
concerns: She is worried that cutting off another facial bump will leave a noticeable scar right before her college graduation.
expectations: She hopes the doctor can recommend a scarless laser treatment or a gentle cream to make it go away without surgery.
pmh: Multiple prior similar skin lesions removed since her early teens; family history of early-onset skin cancers

clinical_knowledge.topic: Basal Cell Carcinoma evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Basal Cell Carcinoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes biopsy confirmation, evaluation for an underlying predisposing syndrome given the young age, and referral for Mohs micrographic surgery, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: pearly white facial nodule with telangiectasias

Key HPI features: A 20-year-old female presents with a pearly white facial nodule with telangiectasias, similar to several other small lesions she has had removed from her face and trunk since her early teens. She reports a family history of early-onset skin cancers.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. Pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasias on the face; multiple healed scars from prior lesion excisions on the face and trunk. Screen for macrocephaly, frontal bossing, and palmar/plantar pitting.
Relevant background/PMH: Multiple prior similar skin lesions removed since her early teens; family history of early-onset skin cancers
common_misconceptions: Assuming BCC only occurs in older, sun-damaged patients and missing early-onset presentations related to Gorlin (nevoid basal cell carcinoma) syndrome or other predisposing conditions.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Squamous cell carcinoma without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Central ulceration (rodent ulcer).
management_principles: BCC is rare in patients this young without a predisposing factor; evaluate for Gorlin (nevoid basal cell carcinoma) syndrome given the history of multiple lesions since her early teens
Confirm the diagnosis with a shave or punch biopsy before definitive treatment
Screen for syndromic features (odontogenic keratocysts, palmar/plantar pits, macrocephaly, rib anomalies) and consider genetics referral (e.g., PTCH1 testing) if suspicion is high
Refer for Mohs micrographic surgery once confirmed given the facial location, and arrange long-term dermatologic surveillance given the elevated risk of additional BCCs.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: A 20-year-old female presents with a pearly white facial nodule with telangiectasias, similar to several other small lesions she has had removed from her face and trunk since her early teens, with a family history of early-onset skin cancers.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasias on the face; multiple healed scars from prior lesion excisions on the face and trunk. No macrocephaly, frontal bossing, or palmar/plantar pitting noted on screening exam.
reference_soap.assessment: Facial nodule with classic pearly, telangiectatic features suggestive of basal cell carcinoma; the young age and history of multiple prior similar lesions raise concern for an underlying predisposing syndrome (e.g., Gorlin/basal cell nevus syndrome) rather than sporadic sun-related BCC.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm with a shave or punch biopsy. Given the young age and lesion history, screen for features of Gorlin syndrome (odontogenic keratocysts via dental imaging, palmar/plantar pits, macrocephaly, rib anomalies) and consider genetics referral. Refer for Mohs micrographic surgery once confirmed, counsel on strict sun protection, and arrange long-term dermatologic surveillance.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Basal Cell Carcinoma face, including when young-onset or multiple BCCs warrant evaluation for Gorlin (nevoid basal cell carcinoma) syndrome
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Basal Cell Carcinoma face
Implement evidence-based management plan: Excisional biopsy, refer for Mohs micrographic surgery

teaching.one_liner: Most common non-melanoma skin cancer presenting as a translucent, pearly papule with telangiectasias.

must_ask.say: Did this skin bump start as a smooth pearly nodule with visible tiny blood vessels?
Does the lesion bleed easily when touched or develop a central crust that doesn't heal?
Do you have a history of significant sun exposure or outdoor work?
How slowly has this lesion expanded over recent time?
Have you ever had skin cancers or precancerous spots removed before?

history.answer: I noticed this small bump on my right cheek a few months ago, and it just won't go away.
I first noticed it about four or five months ago, and it has very slowly become more noticeable.
It is located on my right cheek, right below my lower eyelid.
It started out as a tiny bump and has gradually enlarged to about the size of a small pencil eraser.
It looks shiny and pearly white, and when I look closely I can see tiny branching red blood vessels across it.
It feels like a firm little nodule under my skin, not squishy or fluid-filled.
No, it does not hurt at all, even when I press on it or wash my face.
It bled once after I accidentally scraped it with a washcloth, but usually it does not bleed or crust over.
No, there is no redness around the bump, no warmth, and no pus or drainage.
No, there is no little hole in the center, and no white or cheesy discharge ever comes out.
No, it stays the same size every day and does not swell up or shrink.
No, I have never had an injury, cut, or pimple at that exact spot.
No, the sensation on my face is completely normal, with no numbness, tingling, or weakness.
No fever, chills, night sweats, fatigue, or unexplained weight loss.
No, I haven't noticed any swollen glands in my neck or lumps anywhere else.
I rarely spend time in direct sunlight, I wear SPF 50 sunscreen daily, and I have never had a severe blistering sunburn.
I tried gently squeezing it once thinking it might be a clogged pore, but nothing came out, so I left it alone.
I thought this might just be another one of those harmless cysts or skin bumps that run in my family.
I'm really worried that having another bump removed will leave an obvious scar on my face right before graduation.
I'm hoping there's a laser treatment or a cream that can clear it up without needing to cut my face again.
I have had several similar skin bumps removed from my face and trunk since I was fourteen, which were diagnosed as basal cell carcinomas.
Just the small outpatient minor excisions to remove those previous skin lesions; I have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or dietary supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
My father and older brother have both had multiple basal cell skin cancers removed starting in their early twenties.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any vaping or tobacco products.
I only drink alcohol socially on rare occasions, maybe one glass of wine once a month.
I am a college student living in an apartment near campus with my roommate.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago, my cycles are regular, and there is no chance I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 72/min, respiratory rate 14/min, temperature 36.6°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, well-appearing young female in no distress; head circumference and facial contours appear normal without macrocephaly or frontal bossing.
A 5 mm pearly, translucent nodule with fine branching telangiectasias on the right cheek; multiple well-healed surgical scars on the face and trunk without palmar or plantar pits.
No preauricular, submandibular, or cervical lymphadenopathy palpable bilaterally.
Facial sensation intact across all trigeminal branches, facial movements symmetric, and no cranial nerve deficit.
Oral cavity with normal dentition, intact mucosa, and no palpable jaw swelling or cysts.
